findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider misleadingly returns the default KeyStore provider
findings.body: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is not actually the BouncyCastle provider in most environments (it's whatever the default KeyStore provider is, e.g. SUN). This is semantically wrong for a method whose contract is to return a BouncyCastle-based security provider, and any caller relying on getBouncyCastleProvider() to get BC capabilities will get an unrelated provider, potentially causing subtle failures or wrong algorithm lookups downstream.

findings.title: Dead/wasted ASN1Encoder.create() calls in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: Lines 114-115 create two ASN1Encoder instances and call write() on them, but the results are discarded and never used (the encoder instance is immediately discarded). This is dead code left over from refactoring, wastes allocations and reads confusingly, though it causes no correctness issue since correct encoders are created again on lines 117-121.

findings.title: Removed safety check allows silent selection among multiple CryptoProviders
findings.body: The previous behavior threw an IllegalStateException when multiple CryptoProvider implementations were found on the classpath, forcing developers to notice and resolve ambiguous crypto configurations. This PR replaces that with silent ordering/sorting by order(), picking the highest order and merely logging (at debug level) which providers were ignored. If a deployment accidentally has two crypto providers on the classpath (e.g. due to a dependency misconfiguration), it will silently pick one based on order value instead of failing fast, which could lead to the wrong crypto provider being used in production without any visible warning (debug logging is typically disabled).

findings.title: CryptoIntegration.init called without checking for pre-existing/conflicting provider
findings.body: AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now unconditionally calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()). If the authz-client is used within the main Keycloak server or testsuite (sharing a classloader where both the AuthzClientCryptoProvider and DefaultCryptoProvider service files are visible), detectProvider will pick whichever has higher order (DefaultCryptoProvider order=200 > AuthzClientCryptoProvider order=100), but since CryptoIntegration.init is a once-only init guarded by a null check, if some other code path already initialized CryptoIntegration with a different provider before AuthzClient.create is called, this call becomes a no-op, silently keeping the previous provider. This ordering/initialization-order dependency is fragile and not well documented; combined with the lack of multiple-provider detection warnings, it can result in using the wrong CryptoProvider in mixed classpath scenarios without any error.
